claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by lattice distortion arising from atomic size mismatches.
Lattice distortion enhances dislocation pinning and restricts dislocation mobility.
Composition can be systematically varied to alter atomic size mismatch while processing conditions and grain size are held constant.
The comparison is intended to retain a single-phase state without significant phase separation or precipitation.
Increased lattice strain fields can serve as sites for dislocation pinning.
Increasing atomic size differences among constituent elements produces greater lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion creates local strain fields that hinder dislocation motion.
Hindered dislocation motion increases hardness and yield strength.
Alloys with greater induced lattice distortion will have higher hardness than a baseline alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch.
Alloys with greater induced lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than a baseline alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch.
A baseline HEA formulated to minimize atomic size differences should have lower hardness and strength under otherwise identical test conditions.
The proposed mechanism should dominate in single-phase HEAs when dislocation-mediated plasticity is the primary deformation mode.
The proposed mechanism may not dominate in multiphase alloys or when precipitation hardening or grain-boundary strengthening is significant.
Short-range ordering, grain-size variation, and secondary-phase formation may also affect the measured mechanical properties.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can be used to quantify the lattice strain relevant to the proposed mediator.
Failure of increased atomic size mismatch to produce systematic increases in lattice distortion, hardness, and yield strength would falsify the hypothesis.
